summaries.example: Imagine saying, “The door cannot open.” That might mean the lock is stuck, so opening is practically impossible. It might instead mean opening it is against a rule. The same word, “cannot,” can point to different reasons.
summaries.summary: The word “cannot” has many jobs. A person may be unable to do something because of a locked door, a law, a game rule, a moral reason, or strong evidence. Philosophy calls ideas about what could or must be the case modality. One useful tool is the idea of possible worlds: complete ways the world might have been. A necessary claim is true in every possible world. A possible claim is true in at least one, and a contingent claim is true in some but not all. The entry focuses especially on two kinds of modality. Epistemic modality concerns what evidence and careful thinking allow us to know. Metaphysical modality concerns what could really have been. For example, before testing, it may be possible for us to wonder whether gold has a certain chemical feature, even if gold could not really have lacked that feature. Some philosophers, called dualists, think epistemic and metaphysical modality are fundamentally different. Monists try to explain the appearances using one kind of modality, perhaps by distinguishing meanings or uses of sentences. The entry also discusses nomic, or natural-law, necessity. Finally, it asks whether all kinds of necessity can be explained using a few basic kinds.
key_ideas: “Cannot” can mean different things: something may be blocked, forbidden, against a game’s rules, or ruled out by evidence.
Possible worlds are tools for thinking about different ways things might have turned out.
A claim can be necessary, possible, or contingent.
Philosophers disagree about whether what must be true and what can be known without evidence are the same.
They also ask whether the laws of nature have their own special kind of necessity.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us notice that “possible,” “necessary,” and “cannot” do not always mean the same thing. That matters in science, everyday reasoning, rules, and arguments. It also helps us separate what the world allows from what our evidence currently supports.

important_terms.definition: A way something could be, must be, or could not be. Words such as “could,” “must,” and “cannot” often show modality.
A complete way the world might have been. Philosophers use possible worlds to compare what is necessary, possible, and contingent.
True in every possible world; it could not have been false.
True in some possible worlds but not all. Something contingent is true, but it could have been different.
Connected with what someone knows or what the evidence allows that person to believe.
Connected with what could really have been the case, not merely with what we know.

questions_to_think_about: When you say “I can’t,” do you mean you are unable, not allowed, or unsure?
Could a rule be changed even when a fact about the world could not be changed?
Is something necessary because of its meaning, because of nature, or for another reason?

summaries.example: Suppose scientists have not yet measured a metal’s atomic number. Before the experiment, several results may be epistemically possible: the evidence does not rule them out. But once the metal is identified as gold, philosophers may argue that having atomic number 79 is metaphysically necessary for gold. On that view, a fact can be necessary even though learning it requires empirical investigation.
summaries.summary: Modality concerns what could be, must be, or could not be. The possible-worlds framework represents maximally specific ways the world might have been. A proposition is metaphysically necessary if it is true in all metaphysically possible worlds, possible if true in at least one, and contingent if true in some but not all. Epistemic modality concerns what an agent’s evidence and ideal reasoning leave open. It is therefore agent-relative unless one considers an ideal agent with no empirical evidence, which yields the notion of the a priori. A central dispute is whether metaphysical necessity and epistemic necessity coincide. Examples associated with Kripke suggest they may come apart: identities involving rigid names, the chemical nature of gold, and the composition of a particular object can appear metaphysically necessary while being knowable only a posteriori. Conversely, a term introduced by a description may generate a claim that seems a priori but not metaphysically necessary. Dualists interpret these cases as evidence for two fundamental modalities and possibly two spaces of worlds. Monists retain one space or one modality, explaining the contrast through two propositions associated with a sentence, through two-dimensional semantics, or through pragmatic communication. The entry then considers natural-law modality. Necessitarians hold that laws are metaphysically necessary; contingentists allow that laws could have been different but may assign them a distinct nomic necessity. Arguments concern causal essentialism and the counterfactual stability of laws. The final issue is the structure of the modal realm: whether kinds such as logical, mathematical, biological, moral, and legal necessity can be reduced to a few fundamental kinds by restriction or relativization.
key_ideas: The same modal word can express practical, moral, legal, logical, evidential, or natural-law constraints.
Possible-worlds analysis defines necessity as truth in all worlds, possibility as truth in some, and contingency as truth in some but not all.
The apparent existence of necessary a posteriori truths challenges the idea that necessity and a priority have exactly the same scope.
Dualists posit distinct epistemic and metaphysical spaces; monists explain the difference through semantics or communication.
Nomic necessity may be metaphysical necessity, or it may be a weaker necessity grounded in the laws of nature.
The entry asks how different modal notions relate and which, if any, are fundamental.
summaries.why_it_matters: Distinguishing kinds of necessity prevents arguments from sliding between “cannot” in different senses. The distinctions are important for interpreting scientific laws, understanding what evidence establishes, analyzing meaning and reference, and deciding whether one unified theory of modality is possible. They also show why a claim’s being necessary is not automatically the same as its being knowable a priori.

important_terms.definition: The study of ways things could be, must be, or could not be; it includes several kinds of necessity and possibility.
A complete, maximally specific way the world could have been, used to analyze possibility and necessity.
A proposition is necessary when it is true in every relevant possible world; metaphysical necessity concerns what could genuinely have been the case.
A proposition is epistemically necessary for an agent when that agent’s evidence plus ideal reasoning rules out its negation.
Knowledge independent of empirical evidence, at least in the relevant sense. The entry examines whether every necessary truth is a priori.
Knowledge that depends on experience or empirical investigation.
A necessity associated with the laws of nature. Contingentists treat it as distinct from metaphysical necessity; necessitarians do not.
The view that epistemic and metaphysical modality are fundamentally distinct; monism instead seeks a one-modality explanation.

questions_to_think_about: If a claim is true in every metaphysically possible world, must it be knowable without experience?
Does the fact that a law is counterfactually robust support necessitarianism?
Can a difference in sentence meaning explain the appearance of two kinds of modality?
What would make a kind of necessity fundamental rather than merely derived?
Are moral or legal requirements kinds of necessity in the same sense as metaphysical necessity?

summaries.example: A detective may say, “Sam cannot be in the library,” because a video shows Sam elsewhere. That is an epistemic claim: the evidence rules out the library story. A locked library door would create a practical obstacle instead. A chess rule could make castling impossible in a position, while a fact about someone’s identity might make another situation impossible in a deeper sense. One sentence can use “cannot” for different reasons.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the many meanings of modal language. Saying that something “cannot” happen might report a contradiction in meaning, an essential feature of an object, a law of nature, a technological limitation, a practical barrier, a moral or legal requirement, a game rule, or what the evidence establishes. These differences motivate a general philosophical theory of modality. Possible worlds provide one framework. A proposition is necessary when true in all relevant worlds, possible when true in at least one, and contingent when true in some but not all. The main debate in the first part concerns epistemic and metaphysical modality. Epistemic necessity depends on an agent’s evidence and ideal reasoning. Metaphysical necessity concerns what could really have been. The two may diverge: a statement about the identity of two names or the chemical nature of gold may be necessary, yet learning it may require observation. A description can also make a statement seem knowable without investigation even though the described person or object could have had a different career or role. Dualists take such cases to show that epistemic and metaphysical modality are fundamentally different. Monists argue that one underlying modal system can explain the appearance of a difference. Their proposals appeal either to multiple propositions associated with one sentence, to different ways of evaluating a sentence across worlds, or to how speakers communicate in context. The entry also considers whether natural laws have nomic necessity. Necessitarians identify this with metaphysical necessity, while contingentists treat it as a distinct, often weaker form. The final section asks how logical, mathematical, biological, moral, and legal necessities might be related to more basic modal ideas.
key_ideas: Modal claims can be true for very different reasons, including meanings, evidence, nature, technology, rules, morality, and law.
Possible worlds help distinguish necessity, possibility, and contingency.
Epistemic possibility depends on an agent’s information, while metaphysical possibility concerns what could really have happened.
Cases that seem necessary but discoverable only through experience challenge the equation of necessity with a priori knowledge.
The debate between dualism and monism concerns whether there are two fundamental modal systems or one.
Natural laws may have a special nomic necessity, or they may be metaphysically necessary after all.
summaries.why_it_matters: These distinctions make philosophical and scientific reasoning more careful. They help us ask whether a statement concerns reality, evidence, language, rules, or norms. They also clarify why discovering a fact through experiment does not by itself show that the fact could have been otherwise.

important_terms.definition: Talk about what is possible, necessary, or impossible. Modal words include “could,” “must,” and “cannot.”
A fully described way the world might have been. Possible worlds are a philosophical comparison tool, not necessarily separate physical places.
True in all relevant possible worlds; there is no way for it to be false under that kind of modality.
True in some relevant possible worlds and false in others; it could have been otherwise.
A kind of modality concerning evidence, knowledge, and which possibilities an agent can rule out.
A kind of modality concerning what could genuinely have been the case, including the essential features of things.
A proposed necessity associated with laws of nature, such as laws governing motion.
The view that epistemic and metaphysical necessity are different; monism explains their apparent difference with one underlying modality.

questions_to_think_about: Can the same event be epistemically possible but metaphysically impossible?
Why might a law of nature be more stable under imagined changes than an accidental pattern?
When a name is introduced using a description, does the description determine its meaning or merely its reference?
Is explaining two modal notions with one theory always simpler?
Which kinds of necessity, if any, seem basic rather than derived?
